header.title: Software Architecture and Product Engineering
header.lead: I help teams design and build software systems that can survive real use: changing requirements, growing teams, operational pressure, and the long memory of code.

data.text: This capability comes from a double practice: academic work in software engineering and hands-on involvement in real products. I have worked around modular monoliths, microservice ecosystems, gateways, identity modules, document workflows, process-oriented application generation, mobile backends, and business platforms where maintainability matters as much as the first delivery.

rows: The product is growing faster than its architecture.
Clarify bounded contexts, identify modules, define dependency rules, and separate domain, application, infrastructure, and presentation concerns.
A team must modernize without stopping delivery.
Propose incremental migration paths, preserve working behavior, reduce risky rewrites, and create technical milestones that can be verified.
The system is hard to explain to new developers.
Produce architecture maps, module descriptions, onboarding documentation, code conventions, and examples of expected implementation style.
A product idea needs to become buildable.
Translate business goals into use cases, APIs, data models, screens, workflows, and a technical roadmap.
Introduce testing strategy, review discipline, traceability, refactoring habits, and release criteria from the design stage.

items: Domain model, module map, and dependency rules.
API contracts, technical specifications, and implementation guidelines.
Prototype or reference implementation for a sensitive module.
Testing strategy, quality gates, and release-readiness checklist.
[b]Architecture should explain the business[/b]: modules must reflect real responsibilities, not only technical layers.
[b]A system should be easy to change in the expected directions[/b]: design is judged by future work, not only by today's elegance.
[b]Trade-offs must be explicit[/b]: performance, cost, maintainability, security, delivery speed, and team skill are all part of the architecture.
[b]Code is a social artifact[/b]: naming, structure, tests, and documentation determine how a team thinks together.
[b]Research matters when it becomes practical[/b]: workflow modeling, process execution, service orientation, and formal reasoning are useful when they clarify the product.

rows: Domain-driven design, hexagonal architecture, modular monoliths, microservices, API gateways, service-oriented systems, BPMN/process modeling.
Java/Spring Boot, Maven, Liquibase, PHP/Laravel, .NET, Node.js, REST APIs, identity, notification, document, billing, and reporting modules.
JUnit, Cucumber, JaCoCo, Jest, Pest, code review, refactoring, test-support modules, integration tests, release gates.
Architecture notes, system maps, runbooks, README standards, onboarding material, technical decision records.
